name: Verdance Falling
geological_features: Broad temperate river valleys flanked by ancient granite mountain ranges
Extensive limestone cave systems beneath the equatorial forests
Fertile volcanic plains fed by now-dormant shield volcanoes
specific_features: Vast old-growth forests showing accelerating dieback from an unidentified blight
Megafauna species in sharp population decline over the past century
Atmospheric pollen counts dropping to historically unprecedented lows
description: Verdance Falling is a terrestrial world of heartbreaking beauty, its continents draped in forests of towering broadleaf canopy, threaded with silver rivers, and crowned by snow-capped mountain ranges that catch the light of a warm yellow sun. The climate is mild and generous, the soil deep and fertile, the oceans clean and teeming. By every metric it should be a paradise, and for most of its four-billion-year history, it was.

Something is wrong. The forests are thinning in patterns that do not match any natural cycle, their canopies browning and collapsing inward from the heartwood. The great migration herds that once darkened the plains have dwindled to scattered remnants, their calving rates plummeting for reasons xenobiologists cannot yet identify. The air still smells of green growth and clean rain, but beneath it there is a faint, sour undertone that automated sensors flag but cannot classify.

Verdance Falling was first surveyed forty standard years ago and immediately flagged as an ecological treasure, its biosphere dense with unique compounds of pharmaceutical interest. Early harvesting permits were granted to three biotech firms before the decline became apparent. Whether the harvesting operations triggered or merely coincided with the blight remains the subject of furious scientific and legal debate, with billions in liability hanging on the answer.

Conservation teams now race against a collapse they do not fully understand, establishing gene banks and protected reserves while the political machinery of quarantine enforcement grinds slowly forward. The megafauna are the most visible casualties, their dwindling herds tracked by satellite with grim precision, but the true crisis may lie in the soil microbiome where preliminary analysis suggests a fundamental disruption at the base of the food web. Verdance Falling is a world in the act of dying, and the window to save it narrows with each passing season.
